description:
We’re students with hands-on experience in deep research, AI-assisted coding, software engineering, web development, and graphic design. With Apex Fire, we’re exploring how data and technology can make wildfire monitoring more accessible and understandable.

Join us if you enjoy researching deeply, experimenting, and building things that matter. We’re looking for teammates interested in data analysis, mapping/GIS, backend development, or environmental science—and curious, motivated people.
summary:
ApexFire turns satellite fire data into a shared workspace for everyday users and specialists. Built in two days, our working web prototype combines NASA MODIS and VIIRS hotspots, weather, historical records and real fire stories in one accessible application.

Everyday users can explore recent satellite detections, check nearby settlements and weather, follow activity and share what they see. Experts can investigate more than two decades of observations, compare sensors, inspect evidence and export filtered data with its sources.

We address the harmonization challenge by combining a burning-activity calendar with a prototype method that compares MODIS and VIIRS on a common spatial and temporal basis, with conversions evaluated on years excluded from training.

North Macedonia is our proving ground: a focused place to develop the features, examine real incidents and build partnerships before expanding region by region. Two days produced a working foundation. With fire scientists, emergency professionals and local communities, that foundation could become a global hub for understanding fire activity, supporting research and strengthening preparedness.
details:
Fire information becomes useful when people can understand it, examine its evidence and apply it to the places they care about. ApexFire brings those needs together in one web application, with Simple and Expert modes serving different levels of knowledge.

For everyday users

A resident can search for their town, explore recent satellite sightings of heat, see nearby settlements and check weather and weather-based fire danger. Wind visualizations help explain the surrounding conditions, while dated satellite imagery adds context. Users can follow a fire-related area on their device and share a link to the same view, without creating an account.

This makes ApexFire useful for regular awareness: checking activity around a home, a village or a place someone plans to visit, then returning to see what changed. Following currently counts new detections when the app loads; phone and email alerts are a future development.

For experts: an evidence and data hub

Expert mode exposes the underlying observations: dates, satellite and sensor, native confidence values, fire radiative power, filters and coverage information. An archive spanning 2000–2026 connects a map, calendar and historical weather context. Researchers, journalists and land-management professionals can investigate seasonal patterns, compare periods and explore documented incidents.

Filtered observations can be exported as CSV or GeoJSON, alongside provenance describing sources, filters and transformations. The data can therefore leave the interface and support further work in spreadsheets, GIS software or research workflows.

Fire stories connect satellite detections, mapped burned areas, weather and imagery. Brvenica's observed progression and the Mariovo evidence study show how different sources can be examined together, including where they disagree. Spread Lab adds a real experimental surface-fire model run as a foundation for future scenario research.

Our response to the MODIS–VIIRS challenge

Different sensors can produce different hotspot counts even when observing similar burning activity. A more sensitive sensor should not automatically make the historical record look like a sudden increase in fire.

ApexFire aggregates detections into common spatial cells and UTC days, then fits prototype conversions between MODIS and VIIRS activity totals. It evaluates those conversions on later years excluded from training and publishes the resulting errors and limitations. The calendar and sensor-comparison tools help users explore when and where activity occurred, while the harmonization layer investigates comparability across sensor generations.

Why North Macedonia comes first

North Macedonia is our initial development and validation setting. A focused national scope lets us examine historical incidents, understand data gaps and improve the experience with people who know the terrain and local needs. It gives us a practical way to refine the system before broadening its geographic scope.

Many underlying satellite datasets already cover the world. Our path to a global ApexFire is regional expansion backed by local evaluation: testing sensor relationships, adding appropriate weather, terrain and fuel information, and working with regional partners. The current Macedonian conversion is a prototype for this process, rather than an already validated global model.

What two days demonstrated and what comes next

In two days, we connected a public-facing map, historical exploration, sensor comparison, downloadable evidence, incident stories and an experimental model demonstration. That progress shows how quickly accessible Earth-observation data can become a useful working product.

The next leap needs expertise as well as development. Fire scientists can challenge the methods; emergency professionals can define useful workflows; local institutions can contribute observations and evaluate outputs; communities can test whether the information is understandable. Those partnerships could turn a promising prototype into a dependable tool for research, public awareness and preparedness.

Technology and design choices

We used TypeScript, React, Vite and MapLibre GL JS for the interface; Python and geospatial libraries for data preparation and analysis; Firebase Cloud Functions and Realtime Database for scheduled ingestion; and Pyretechnics for the experimental spread run. NASA data is combined with Copernicus, ECMWF, Open-Meteo and other credited sources. Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted development, research and review; built-in image generation supported the identity and banner.

We prioritized mobile use, clear language, account-free access, portable exports, source traceability and visible uncertainty. The live ingestion checks for new FIRMS data every 15 minutes; this is our refresh interval, not a promise of immediate satellite detection. Hotspots are observations of heat, not automatically confirmed wildfires. The spread demonstration is experimental, and operational emergency use requires professional validation and an operating partner.
